analysis.one_liner: Makes offshore oil companies pay the full cost of spills instead of a $75 million cap.
analysis.headline: The bill to lift the $75 million cap on offshore oil spill liability never got a hearing or a vote and died in committee after two subcommittee referrals.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Oil Pollution Act of 1990, a company responsible for an offshore oil spill owes its cleanup costs plus at most $75 million in damages. This bill would strike that dollar cap, so an offshore driller that fouls coastal waters would owe whatever the damage actually costs. It would even apply the change retroactively to April 15, 2010, days before the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion. The bill was referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and then to its Coast Guard subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Coastal residents, fishing and seafood businesses, tourism operators, and taxpayers. Removing the cap means the company that causes a spill, not the public, bears the full cost of the damage. It also protects taxpayers from ever being asked to cover spill costs that exceed the capped liability, the scenario the bill's 'bailout prevention' title targets.

how_it_helps.text: Strikes the Oil Pollution Act provision that limits a responsible party's liability for an offshore facility discharge to removal costs plus $75 million, leaving no dollar cap on what a spiller owes.
Conforms a related provision so the limit on liability is fully removed for offshore facilities other than deepwater ports.

Makes the change retroactive to April 15, 2010, which places the effective date before the Deepwater Horizon rig explosion of April 20, 2010, the spill that showed a major offshore disaster can cost many billions of dollars, far beyond the cap.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies and their investors, who would face uncapped liability for spill damage. Higher insurance and risk costs for offshore drilling would in time feed into energy prices, and operators that cannot insure unlimited risk might cut back or sell to larger competitors.
analysis.who_pays_short: Offshore oil drillers and their investors

drawbacks.text: Uncapped liability is difficult to insure against; the change could push smaller offshore operators out of the market or concentrate drilling among the largest companies, potentially raising costs that flow to consumers.

The retroactive effective date of April 15, 2010 applies new legal liability to conduct that occurred before the bill was written, a fairness objection an honest supporter of retroactive liability would have to answer.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is sound for the public: a $75 million cap is a fraction of what a major offshore disaster costs, so leaving it in place quietly shifts spill losses toward taxpayers and claimants. The serious defects are the retroactive effective date, which applies new law to old conduct, and the practical effect that uncapped risk may concentrate offshore drilling among the biggest firms rather than spread it across the industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Coast Guard subcommittee for the entire two-year Congress and was never scheduled for a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rush Holt introduced the bill on January 26, 2011 with 19 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation, and the record shows no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
The bill attracted 24 cosponsors in total, all Democrats, and never reached the floor of the Republican-controlled House before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas companies came out ahead: the $75 million cap on their spill liability stayed in place for the whole Congress, and they never had to face a vote on paying the full cost of their own disasters. Taxpayers and coastal residents remain exposed to spill losses beyond what capped liability would cover.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Offshore oil drillers keep the liability cap

for.what_they_did: Introduced the Big Oil Bailout Prevention Act on January 26, 2011 to remove the offshore spill liability cap.

against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral, sent it to the Coast Guard and Maritime Transportation subcommittee, and took no further action; no hearing or markup was ever held.

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats and the sponsor was a Democrat; with Republicans holding the House majority and the committee chair, the bill never advanced, and no Republican cosponsored it.

industries.note: The bill would replace the current cap of removal costs plus $75 million with unlimited liability for offshore spills, so drillers and their insurers would bear the full cost of any disaster they cause. The industry's interest in keeping the cap runs directly against coastal residents and taxpayers, who absorb spill costs beyond the cap.

industries.industry: Coastal fishing, seafood, and tourism businesses
industries.note: Removing the cap means businesses and residents harmed by an offshore spill can recover full damages from the responsible party rather than being cut off at the statutory limit. Their recovery aligns with the public's interest in polluters paying.
Uncapped driller liability would create demand for far larger offshore liability coverage, expanding the market for underwriters, while making them the channel through which spill risk is priced.
